blocks.en: The Most Offensive Verse
blocks.es_reference: El Versículo Más Ofensivo

blocks.en: We come now to the hardest thing a Christian has to say in a roomful of his neighbors. When Thomas asked the Lord how they could know the way, Jesus did not hand him a map or a list of rules. He said something far more startling: "I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me." In a world that prizes nothing higher than tolerance, this is the verse that draws blood. Jesus is not offering one path among many up the same mountain; He is claiming to be the only door. Many a believer, feeling the heat of the room, has quietly let that claim slip, and even some who name the name of Christ will say, with a shrug, that surely all religions are equally good and all roads lead to God. So we must think clearly here, with both backbone and kindness, for this is the point on which the modern heart most stumbles.
blocks.es_reference: Llegamos ahora a lo más difícil que un cristiano tiene que decir en una sala llena de sus vecinos. Cuando Tomás le preguntó al Señor cómo podían conocer el camino, Jesús no le entregó un mapa ni una lista de reglas. Dijo algo mucho más sorprendente: "Yo soy el camino, la verdad y la vida; nadie viene al Padre, sino por mí." En un mundo que no estima nada más alto que la tolerancia, este es el versículo que saca sangre. Jesús no ofrece un sendero entre muchos por la misma montaña; afirma ser la única puerta. Más de un creyente, sintiendo el calor de la sala, ha dejado escapar calladamente esa afirmación, y aun algunos que llevan el nombre de Cristo dirán, encogiéndose de hombros, que de seguro todas las religiones son igualmente buenas y que todos los caminos llevan a Dios. Así que debemos pensar con claridad aquí, con firmeza y con bondad a la vez, pues este es el punto en el que el corazón moderno más tropieza.

blocks.en: Why "All Roads" Cannot Be True
blocks.es_reference: Por Qué "Todos los Caminos" No Puede Ser Verdad

blocks.en: Begin with simple honesty about what the religions actually say. It has become popular to say that all religions teach essentially the same thing, different roads up the same mountain. But a careful, respectful look at what each tradition actually claims makes that hard to sustain. They do not merely take different roads to the same place; on some of their most basic claims, they describe different places. One faith says there is one God; another says there are thousands; another says there is no God at all. One says you live once and face judgment; another says you return many times on a wheel of rebirth. One says the self must be saved; another says the self must be dissolved or extinguished. These are not simply four ways of saying the same thing. On these specific points they contradict one another, and the plain law of reason tells us that contradictory statements cannot all be true at once, at least not in the same sense at the same time. Notice that we never grow so soft-headed in any other field of knowledge. In the schoolroom we do not let one teacher say that two and two are four and another that two and two are five and then call both of them right; once a law of nature is established, no one pretends that the opposite claim is equally valid. We reserve this strange tolerance for the spiritual realm alone, where we suddenly announce that every map is correct even when they point in opposite directions. But truth is not less exacting in religion than in arithmetic. It is more.
blocks.es_reference: Comience con sencilla honestidad sobre lo que las religiones de verdad dicen. Se ha vuelto popular decir que todas las religiones enseñan esencialmente lo mismo, caminos distintos a la misma montaña. Pero una mirada cuidadosa y respetuosa a lo que cada tradición realmente afirma hace difícil sostener eso. No solo toman caminos distintos al mismo lugar; en algunas de sus afirmaciones más básicas, describen lugares distintos. Una fe dice que hay un Dios; otra dice que hay miles; otra dice que no hay Dios en absoluto. Una dice que vives una vez y enfrentas el juicio; otra dice que regresas muchas veces en una rueda de renacimiento. Una dice que el yo debe ser salvado; otra dice que el yo debe ser disuelto o extinguido. Estas no son simplemente cuatro maneras de decir lo mismo. En estos puntos específicos se contradicen unas a otras, y la simple ley de la razón nos dice que afirmaciones contradictorias no pueden ser todas verdad a la vez, al menos no en el mismo sentido al mismo tiempo. Note que jamás nos volvemos tan blandos de cabeza en ningún otro campo del conocimiento. En el aula no dejamos que un maestro diga que dos y dos son cuatro y otro que dos y dos son cinco y luego llamamos correctos a ambos; una vez establecida una ley de la naturaleza, nadie finge que la afirmación contraria es igualmente válida. Reservamos esta extraña tolerancia solo para el reino espiritual, donde de repente anunciamos que todo mapa es correcto aun cuando apuntan en direcciones opuestas. Pero la verdad no es menos exigente en la religión que en la aritmética. Lo es más.

blocks.en: The Blind Men and the Elephant
blocks.es_reference: Los Ciegos y el Elefante

blocks.en: You will often hear the old story brought out as if it settled the matter. Several blind men lay hold of an elephant; one feels the trunk and says the beast is a snake, another feels the leg and says it is a tree, another the ear and says it is a fan, and so the tale concludes that every religion has hold of one part of the same great truth. It is a charming story, but turn it over and look at the back of it. The whole point of the parable is lost on the one telling it, for how does the narrator know that the blind men are all touching one elephant? Only because he can see the whole animal. The man who says "all religions are blind men touching the same elephant" has quietly seated himself in the one chair in the room that can see, claiming the very thing he says no one can have — a view of the whole truth. The parable that was meant to humble every religion turns out to be the proudest claim of all.
blocks.es_reference: A menudo oirá sacar el viejo cuento como si zanjara el asunto. Varios ciegos se aferran a un elefante; uno toca la trompa y dice que la bestia es una serpiente, otro toca la pata y dice que es un árbol, otro la oreja y dice que es un abanico, y así el cuento concluye que cada religión tiene asida una parte de la misma gran verdad. Es un cuento encantador, pero déle la vuelta y mire el reverso. Todo el sentido de la parábola se le escapa al que la cuenta, pues ¿cómo sabe el narrador que los ciegos tocan todos un mismo elefante? Solo porque él puede ver el animal entero. El hombre que dice "todas las religiones son ciegos que tocan el mismo elefante" se ha sentado calladamente en la única silla de la sala que puede ver, reclamando para sí justo aquello que dice que nadie puede tener — una vista de la verdad entera. La parábola que pretendía humillar a toda religión resulta ser la afirmación más orgullosa de todas.

blocks.en: The New Atheist and His Borrowed Sword
blocks.es_reference: El Nuevo Ateo y Su Espada Prestada

blocks.en: In our day a louder voice has joined the chorus, the voice that says all religion is not merely mistaken but poisonous, the great enemy of reason and the cause of the world's cruelty. We should listen to the charge, for the church has indeed sinned and ought to own it honestly. But watch the sword he swings, and ask where its edge comes from. When the atheist thunders that religion is evil, that intolerance is wicked, that the strong ought not to crush the weak, he is wielding a blade of moral judgment. Some atheist philosophers have tried to ground that judgment without appealing to God, arguing that moral facts are simply real features of the universe; that is a serious position, not a bluff, and deserves to be treated as one. But the Christian can still press a fair question: on a purely naturalistic account, where the universe is ultimately just matter in motion with no purpose built in, it is not obvious why moral obligation should exist at all, or why anyone would be bound by it rather than merely preferring it. Scripture already showed us what a whole society looks like when it tries to run on something less than a real, external standard. The book of Judges ends with a chilling refrain, repeated as its final verdict: "every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25). This was not moral freedom; it was moral collapse. Read the chapters that lead to that line — a Levite's concubine abandoned to a mob and left for dead, a civil war that nearly annihilated an entire tribe, men seizing wives by force at a festival because no one could tell them they were wrong. When "right" means nothing more than what each man judges for himself, this is not a hypothetical danger; it is the plain historical record of where it leads. Theism offers a more natural grounding for the very moral law the atheist appeals to — a good and personal God whose character is the standard, not each man's own eyes. His outrage at cruelty is itself worth noticing either way; a man does not rage at a broken world for no reason, and the Christian can ask him where he thinks that sense of "broken," of how things ought to be, ultimately comes from — and whether his own worldview can supply an answer sturdier than the one Judges hands us.
blocks.es_reference: En nuestros días una voz más fuerte se ha unido al coro, la voz que dice que toda religión no solo está equivocada sino que es venenosa, la gran enemiga de la razón y la causa de la crueldad del mundo. Debemos escuchar la acusación, pues la iglesia en verdad ha pecado y debe reconocerlo con honestidad. Pero observe la espada que blande, y pregunte de dónde viene su filo. Cuando el ateo truena que la religión es mala, que la intolerancia es perversa, que el fuerte no debe aplastar al débil, está empuñando una hoja de juicio moral. Algunos filósofos ateos han intentado fundamentar ese juicio sin apelar a Dios, argumentando que los hechos morales son simplemente rasgos reales del universo; esa es una posición seria, no un farol, y merece tratarse como tal. Pero el cristiano todavía puede plantear una pregunta justa: en un relato puramente naturalista, donde el universo es en última instancia solo materia en movimiento sin propósito incorporado, no es obvio por qué la obligación moral debería existir en absoluto, o por qué alguien estaría atado a ella en vez de simplemente preferirla. La Escritura ya nos mostró cómo luce una sociedad entera cuando intenta funcionar con algo menos que una norma real y externa. El libro de Jueces termina con un estribillo escalofriante, repetido como su veredicto final: "cada uno hacía lo que bien le parecía" (Jueces 21:25). Esto no era libertad moral; era colapso moral. Lea los capítulos que llevan a esa línea — la concubina de un levita abandonada a una turba y dejada por muerta, una guerra civil que casi aniquiló a una tribu entera, hombres tomando esposas por la fuerza en una fiesta porque nadie podía decirles que estaban equivocados. Cuando "lo correcto" no significa más que lo que cada hombre juzga por sí mismo, esto no es un peligro hipotético; es el simple registro histórico de a dónde conduce. El teísmo ofrece un fundamento más natural para la misma ley moral a la que apela el ateo — un Dios bueno y personal cuyo carácter es la norma, no los propios ojos de cada hombre. Su indignación ante la crueldad vale la pena notarla de cualquier modo; un hombre no se enfurece ante un mundo roto sin razón, y el cristiano puede preguntarle de dónde cree que en última instancia viene ese sentido de lo "roto", de cómo deberían ser las cosas — y si su propia cosmovisión puede ofrecer una respuesta más firme que la que Jueces nos entrega.

blocks.en: The One Religion That Runs Backward
blocks.es_reference: La Única Religión que Corre al Revés

blocks.en: But the deepest answer to "all roads are the same" is simply to set the roads side by side and look. In broad strokes, most of the major religious paths outside Christianity center on human effort reaching toward the divine — keep these laws, say these prayers, purify yourself through discipline or many lives — even though a fair reading of each tradition also finds real currents of mercy and divine grace within it: Buddhism's Pure Land schools trust entirely in Amida Buddha's grace rather than self-effort, devotional Hindu bhakti movements lean on a god's grace rather than merit, and Islam names God's mercy (rahma) among His central attributes. So the contrast is a matter of emphasis and center of gravity, not an absolute line with grace on one side and none on the other. Still, the emphasis in the gospel is distinctive in its own right. The good news of Christ centers not on our reaching up but on God reaching down. It is the message in which God does the climbing down: while other traditions, even at their most grace-centered, generally still ask something of us to appropriate or approach that grace, the gospel announces that heaven has reached down to us, that God Himself came the whole distance in the person of His Son, and that what we could never earn He freely gives entirely apart from our own effort or merit. That is not Christianity being simply one more road up the mountain. It is the claim that the mountain itself came down to the valley to carry us home.
blocks.es_reference: Pero la respuesta más profunda a "todos los caminos son iguales" es sencillamente poner los caminos lado a lado y mirar. En trazos amplios, la mayoría de los caminos religiosos importantes fuera del cristianismo se centran en el esfuerzo humano que se extiende hacia lo divino — guarde estas leyes, rece estas oraciones, purifíquese a través de la disciplina o de muchas vidas — aunque una lectura justa de cada tradición también halla corrientes reales de misericordia y gracia divina dentro de ella: las escuelas de la Tierra Pura del budismo confían por completo en la gracia de Amida Buda en lugar del esfuerzo propio, los movimientos devocionales bhakti del hinduismo se apoyan en la gracia de un dios en lugar del mérito, y el islam nombra la misericordia de Dios (rahma) entre Sus atributos centrales. Así que el contraste es una cuestión de énfasis y centro de gravedad, no una línea absoluta con la gracia de un solo lado. Aun así, el énfasis del evangelio es distintivo por derecho propio. Las buenas nuevas de Cristo se centran no en nuestro ascenso sino en el descenso de Dios. Es el mensaje en el que Dios hace el descenso: mientras otras tradiciones, aun en su forma más centrada en la gracia, generalmente todavía piden algo de nosotros para apropiarnos de esa gracia o acercarnos a ella, el evangelio anuncia que el cielo se ha extendido hacia abajo hasta nosotros, que Dios mismo recorrió toda la distancia en la persona de Su Hijo, y que lo que nunca pudimos ganar Él lo da gratuitamente, enteramente aparte de nuestro propio esfuerzo o mérito. Eso no es el cristianismo siendo simplemente un camino más por la montaña. Es la afirmación de que la montaña misma bajó al valle para llevarnos a casa.

blocks.en: The Heart Beneath the Argument
blocks.es_reference: El Corazón Bajo el Argumento

blocks.en: And here we must turn a corner, for I would be a poor teacher if I left you thinking that unbelief is only ever a failure of logic to be cured by a better syllogism. It is often something far more tender than that. A wise man who studied these things observed that behind a great deal of atheism there lies not an argument but a wound, and very often the wound has the shape of a father. I have seen this with my own eyes more than once. I knew a woman who could not bear the word father applied to God, and when at last her story came out, it was this: when she was a girl, her own father, in a fit of cruelty, had killed her little dog before her. How was she to trust a Father in heaven, when the only father she had known had broken her heart? Her unbelief was not really a conclusion; it was a scar. And I knew another, a young person forbidden some ordinary joy of youth by a harsh and religious parent, who walked away from the faith and never came back, not because the arguments had failed but because the home had. I do not tell you these stories to tie them up with a neat bow, for I cannot; the woman, by God's mercy, came at last to the waters of baptism, but the other walked away and is walking still. I tell you only this: when you sit across from a person who says there is no God, you may be looking not at a debater but at a child who was hurt, and the gentleness Peter commanded will do more than any argument you could marshal.
blocks.es_reference: Y aquí debemos doblar una esquina, pues sería un pobre maestro si lo dejara pensando que la incredulidad es siempre solo un fallo de lógica que se cura con un mejor silogismo. A menudo es algo mucho más tierno que eso. Un hombre sabio que estudió estas cosas observó que detrás de gran parte del ateísmo no yace un argumento sino una herida, y muy a menudo la herida tiene la forma de un padre. He visto esto con mis propios ojos más de una vez. Conocí a una mujer que no podía soportar la palabra padre aplicada a Dios, y cuando al fin salió su historia, era esta: cuando era niña, su propio padre, en un arrebato de crueldad, había matado a su perrito delante de ella. ¿Cómo iba a confiar en un Padre en el cielo, cuando el único padre que había conocido le había roto el corazón? Su incredulidad no era en realidad una conclusión; era una cicatriz. Y conocí a otro, un joven a quien un padre duro y religioso le prohibió alguna alegría común de la juventud, y se apartó de la fe y nunca volvió, no porque los argumentos hubieran fallado sino porque el hogar había fallado. No le cuento estas historias para atarlas con un lazo pulcro, pues no puedo; la mujer, por la misericordia de Dios, llegó al fin a las aguas del bautismo, pero el otro se apartó y sigue apartado. Le digo solo esto: cuando se siente frente a una persona que dice que no hay Dios, puede estar mirando no a un polemista sino a un niño que fue herido, y la mansedumbre que Pedro ordenó hará más que cualquier argumento que pudiera reunir.

blocks.en: The Door and the Welcome
blocks.es_reference: La Puerta y la Bienvenida

blocks.en: So we hold the hard verse, but we hold it the way our Lord held it. His exclusiveness was never the cold sneer of a club that keeps people out; it was the urgency of a rescuer who knows there is one rope and means for everyone to reach it. He did not say "I am one of the ways" and leave the drowning to choose among currents; He said "I am the way" and threw the only line that reaches the water. The narrowness of the door is the measure of how desperately He wants you through it. And the wonder is that the door, though it is only one, stands wide open, and the welcome on the other side is wider still — wide enough for the woman who could not say the word father, wide enough, should he ever turn back, for the one who walked away. There is one Way, and His arms are open on it. Who do you say that He is?
blocks.es_reference: Así que sostenemos el versículo difícil, pero lo sostenemos como lo sostuvo nuestro Señor. Su exclusividad nunca fue la fría burla de un club que mantiene a la gente afuera; era la urgencia de un rescatador que sabe que hay una sola cuerda y quiere que todos la alcancen. No dijo "yo soy uno de los caminos" y dejó al que se ahogaba escoger entre corrientes; dijo "yo soy el camino" y arrojó la única línea que llega al agua. La estrechez de la puerta es la medida de cuán desesperadamente Él quiere que usted pase por ella. Y la maravilla es que la puerta, aunque es solo una, está de par en par abierta, y la bienvenida del otro lado es más ancha todavía — lo bastante ancha para la mujer que no podía decir la palabra padre, lo bastante ancha, si alguna vez volviera, para el que se apartó. Hay un solo Camino, y sus brazos están abiertos sobre él. ¿Quién dice usted que es Él?

blocks.en: "Nor is there salvation in any other, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." — Acts 4:12

mc.stem: In John 14:6, when Thomas asked how to know the way, Jesus answered:
options: Follow the wise men of every nation
I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through Me
mc.why: Jesus claimed to be the only way to the Father, not one path among many.

mc.stem: The unit argues that the world's major religions:
options: Are simply different roads to the same destination
Make incompatible claims about God, humanity, and salvation that cannot all be true at once
mc.why: The religions differ not just in practice but in their basic claims about God, humanity, and salvation or liberation — claims that genuinely contradict one another.

mc.stem: The unit argues that the religions cannot all be true because they:
options: Flatly contradict one another, and contradictions cannot all be true
mc.why: One God, many gods, no God — these contradict; reason forbids all being true at once.

mc.stem: The unit compares spiritual truth to arithmetic to show that:
options: We would never call two-and-two-is-four and two-and-two-is-five both right
mc.why: We accept exclusive truth in arithmetic but oddly relax it for the spiritual realm.

mc.stem: The parable meant to humble every religion actually becomes:
mc.why: The teller quietly takes the one seat that can see the whole truth.

mc.stem: The unit says that, in broad strokes, most religious paths outside Christianity center on:
options: Human effort reaching toward the divine, even where currents of grace also exist
mc.why: The contrast with the gospel is one of emphasis; the gospel is distinctive in centering entirely on God's initiative rather than ours.

mc.stem: The unit says the gospel differs from all other religions because in it:
options: God does the climbing down to us
mc.why: Every other faith says 'do'; the gospel says 'done.'

mc.stem: The unit summarizes the contrast as: every other faith says 'do,' but the gospel says:
mc.why: What we could never earn, God freely gives — it is finished.

options: A wound, very often shaped like a father
mc.why: A wise observer noted that much atheism hides a wound, not an argument.

sa.prompt: Explain John 14:6 and why the unit calls it the most offensive verse.
sa.model: In John 14:6, when Thomas asked how to know the way, Jesus did not give a map but said, I am the way, the truth, and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through Me. The unit calls this the most offensive verse because in a world that prizes tolerance above all, this exclusive claim draws blood. Jesus is not offering one path among many up the same mountain; He claims to be the only door to God. Many believers, feeling the heat of the room, quietly let the claim slip, and even some who name Christ shrug and say all religions are equally good. So the unit insists we must think clearly here, holding the exclusive truth of Christ with both backbone and kindness, because this is the point where the modern heart most stumbles.

One says there is one God, another many gods, another no God; one says you live once and face judgment, another that you return many times. On these specific points they contradict one another, and the law of reason says contradictory claims cannot all be true at once, at least not in the same sense at the same time. The unit points out that we never grow so soft in any other field: in arithmetic we do not call two-and-two-is-four and two-and-two-is-five both right. We reserve this strange tolerance for the spiritual realm alone, yet truth is not less exacting in religion than in arithmetic but more.

sa.prompt: Explain the unit's reply to the blind-men-and-the-elephant parable.
sa.model: The parable says several blind men touch one elephant, one calling the trunk a snake, another the leg a tree, and concludes that every religion holds one part of the same truth. The unit turns it over to look at the back. The whole point is lost on the teller, for how does the narrator know the blind men are all touching one elephant? Only because he himself can see the whole animal. So the man who says all religions are blind men touching the same elephant has quietly seated himself in the one chair that can see, claiming the very thing he says no one can have, a view of the whole truth. The parable that was meant to humble every religion turns out to be the proudest claim of all, because the teller secretly exempts himself from the blindness he assigns to everyone else.

sa.prompt: Explain the unit's answer to the New Atheist's charge that religion is evil.
sa.model: The unit first grants that the church has sinned and ought to own it honestly. But then it watches the sword the New Atheist swings, for it is not his own. When he thunders that religion is evil, that intolerance is wicked, and that the strong ought not crush the weak, he is wielding a blade of moral judgment, and on his own account the universe is only matter in motion with no real good or evil, only what survives. In such a world the words wicked and evil have no weight. So he has reached into the Christian's house and pulled down the moral law of right and wrong, then turned it against the house he took it from. He cannot condemn the world's cruelty without borrowing the very moral standard that points to the God he denies. His outrage is itself a witness, for a man does not rage at a broken world unless he carries a memory of how the world ought to be.

sa.prompt: Explain the unit's central contrast: the one religion that 'runs backward.'
sa.model: The unit says the deepest answer to all roads being the same is to set them side by side and look. In broad strokes, most religious paths outside Christianity center on human effort reaching toward the divine — laws, prayers, rituals, or many lives — even though a fair reading finds real currents of grace within several traditions too. The gospel's distinctiveness is a matter of center of gravity: it is the one message centered entirely on God doing the climbing down rather than asking us to climb up. The gospel announces that heaven reached down to us, that God Himself came the whole distance in His Son, and that what we could never earn He gives entirely as a free gift of grace, apart from our own effort. Every other faith centers on do; the gospel says done. So Christianity is not simply one more road up the mountain but the claim that the mountain itself came down to the valley to carry us home.

sa.prompt: Explain why the unit says unbelief is often a wound rather than an argument, using the testimonies.
sa.model: The unit warns the apologist not to treat unbelief as only a failure of logic to be cured by a better syllogism, for it is often far more tender. A wise observer noted that behind much atheism lies not an argument but a wound, very often shaped like a father. The unit gives two examples seen firsthand. One woman could not bear to call God Father, because as a girl her own father, in cruelty, had killed her little dog before her; her unbelief was not a conclusion but a scar, though by God's mercy she came at last to baptism. Another young person, forbidden an ordinary joy by a harsh religious parent, walked away from the faith and is walking still, not because the arguments failed but because the home did. The lesson is that the person who says there is no God may be not a debater but a child who was hurt, so the gentleness Peter commanded does more than any argument.

sa.prompt: Why does the unit tell these two testimonies without tying them up neatly?
sa.model: The unit deliberately refuses to tie the two stories up with a neat bow, because that would be dishonest. One testimony ends in mercy: the woman who could not say the word Father came at last to the waters of baptism. But the other does not resolve: the young person forbidden a youthful joy walked away from the faith and is walking still. Cook tells both truthfully rather than forcing a happy ending onto the second, because real life does not always resolve and a teacher who pretends otherwise loses trust. The honest telling carries its own lesson, that an unbeliever may be a child who was hurt rather than a debater to be defeated, and that the gentleness Peter commanded will do more than triumphant argument. Leaving the second story open also keeps the door of prayer open for the one who walked away.

sa.prompt: How does the unit describe the right spirit of Jesus' exclusiveness?
sa.model: The unit says we must hold the hard verse the way our Lord held it. His exclusiveness was never the cold sneer of a club that keeps people out; it was the urgency of a rescuer who knows there is only one rope and means for everyone to reach it. He did not say I am one of the ways and leave the drowning to choose among currents; He said I am the way and threw the only line that reaches the water. So the narrowness of the door is not meanness but the measure of how desperately He wants every person through it. And the wonder is that the one door stands wide open, with a welcome on the other side that is wider still, wide enough for the woman who could not say Father and, should he ever turn back, for the one who walked away. There is one Way, and His arms are open on it.

sa.prompt: How does Acts 4:12 frame the unit's conclusion?
sa.model: Acts 4:12 declares that there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved. This frames the unit's conclusion by stating plainly that the exclusiveness of Christ is not a harsh add-on but the apostolic gospel itself: salvation is found only in the name of Jesus. The unit holds this exclusive claim together with a wide welcome, presenting the one Way not as a club that shuts people out but as the single rope thrown to the drowning. So the narrow door and the open arms belong together. Acts 4:12 closes the case the same way John 14:6 opened it, with one Savior and one name, and it returns the reader to the course question of who Jesus is, urging that the only name that saves be received rather than merely debated.

sa.prompt: Summarize the unit's overall case about other religions and worldviews.
sa.model: The unit's overall case is that Christ's exclusive claim in John 14:6 is true and must be held with backbone and kindness. The popular idea that all roads lead to God fails because, on their most basic claims, the religions genuinely contradict one another, and contradictions cannot all be true, just as we never call opposite arithmetic answers both right. The blind-men parable secretly claims the very full sight it denies others, and the New Atheist's moral outrage raises a real question about where objective moral obligation is best grounded, with theism offering a more natural answer than naturalism does. Most importantly, the gospel is distinctive in its center of gravity: instead of centering on our climbing toward God, it centers on God climbing down to us in grace, saying done rather than do. Yet the unit also turns to the heart, warning that unbelief is often a wound shaped like a father rather than an argument, so the apologist meets it with gentleness. The one Way is held together with a wide welcome, and the closing question remains who Jesus is.
